opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it should play a central role, and it's one that's been badly underappreciated. A lot of the uncertainty quantification literature treats data as if it fell from the sky: you have a sample, you assume it's i.i.d. from some distribution, and then you put error bars around your predictions. But in the real world data comes from somewhere. It was collected by someone, for some purpose, under some conditions, often filtered through an economic or institutional process. Those facts bear on how much you should trust any statement you make downstream.

Take conformal prediction, which I've worked on quite a bit. Its guarantees rest on exchangeability. That's a beautiful, minimal assumption compared with full parametric modeling, but it's still an assumption about provenance. If your calibration data came from one hospital and you deploy at another, or the data was gathered before some policy change, exchangeability fails and your coverage guarantee can quietly evaporate. So much of the recent work on distribution shift, weighted conformal methods and so on is really about bringing provenance back into the picture: modeling where the data came from relative to where you'll use it.

This connects to something I care about more broadly. I don't think of machine learning as just a single agent fitting a model. It's increasingly a market-like system with many participants: people who provide data, people who label it, platforms that aggregate it, decision makers who consume predictions. Each has incentives. Data can be strategically generated, selectively reported or contaminated. If you ignore that, your uncertainty statements are about a fiction. A real uncertainty quantification should reflect not just sampling noise but how the data was generated and by whom.

There's also a nice opportunity here. In prediction-powered inference we combine a small amount of gold-standard, carefully provenanced data with a large amount of machine-generated predictions, and get valid confidence intervals that are tighter than using the gold data alone. That only works because we know which data is which. Provenance there isn't a nuisance; it's what lets you combine sources honestly. So I'd argue provenance should be a first-class object, tracked and reasoned about just as we track model parameters. It's the bridge between the statistics, which gives you guarantees under assumptions, and the engineering reality, which determines whether those assumptions hold.

And frankly, as more of the data out there is itself generated by models, this becomes urgent. If you can't tell whether a data point came from a human, a sensor or a previous version of an LLM, you can't meaningfully say how uncertain you are. You've lost the thread back to the world.

r001.rationale: The response says provenance and distribution shifts affect trust and that exchangeability can fail after a policy change, but it does not state that older source data should increase the uncertainty attached to an estimate.

r002.rationale: It proposes tracking provenance as a first-class object, but does not specifically propose carrying metadata about data age as the data moves through a larger system.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it should play a central role, and the reason it doesn't yet is that we've inherited a somewhat impoverished way of thinking about uncertainty from classical statistics. The classical story is that you have a data-generating distribution, you have an estimator, and uncertainty is about the sampling variability of that estimator. That's a fine story for a single scientist running a single experiment. It's not the story we're living in.

The data that goes into these large systems comes from many sources, collected by many agents, under many different conditions, for many different reasons. Some of it was collected carefully. Some of it was scraped. Some of it was produced by people who had an incentive to shape what the system would learn. If you throw all of that into a single pool and then compute a confidence interval or a conformal prediction set as if it came from one exchangeable distribution, you're making an assumption that is false, and you've lost the information you'd need to know how false it is.

So provenance, to me, is really about restoring that structure. Where did this come from, who collected it, what was the mechanism, what were the incentives? Once you have that, you can start to do something principled. You can ask whether the data relevant to this particular prediction, for this particular individual, actually supports the level of confidence you're reporting. You can condition your uncertainty on the source rather than averaging over sources. And you can build systems that are honest about the fact that for some queries they are extrapolating from thin or untrustworthy evidence.

I'd also say there's an economic dimension here that I care about a lot. Data has value, and the people who produce it are participants in a system, not just a substrate. If you track provenance, you can in principle attribute value back to sources, which gives people reasons to contribute good data rather than noise. That links the statistics problem to the mechanism design problem, and I think those have to be solved together. Uncertainty quantification that ignores where the data came from is really just uncertainty theater.

r001.rationale: The response discusses conditioning uncertainty on data source and trustworthiness, but never says that older data should increase an estimate’s uncertainty.

r002.rationale: It proposes tracking provenance such as origin, collector, mechanism, and incentives, but does not propose metadata about data age moving through a larger system.

astra-6.text:
I think it should play a central role. Uncertainty isn’t just a property of a collection of numbers. It depends on how those numbers came to be observed: who collected them, what population they sampled, what decisions determined which observations were recorded, and what transformations happened along the way.

You can have a very large dataset and a very narrow confidence interval, and still be answering the wrong question because the data came from a population different from the one you care about. More data doesn’t resolve that problem. Knowing where the data came from at least lets you formulate it.

And provenance matters for dependence. If five sources all repeat an observation from the same original source, you don’t have five independent pieces of evidence. If you lose that history, you can become much more confident than you should be.

So I’d want provenance to inform the assumptions behind uncertainty quantification, rather than simply accompany the final result as documentation. It won’t automatically tell you how much uncertainty to attach to a prediction. But it helps you distinguish what you can estimate from what you’re assuming—and identify where you need more evidence.

r001.rationale: The response discusses provenance and uncertainty generally, but does not say that older source data should increase an estimate’s uncertainty.

r002.rationale: It describes tracking where data came from and how they were transformed, but does not propose carrying metadata about data age through a larger system.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it should play a central role. Uncertainty isn’t just a property of a fitted model. It depends on how the data were collected, who was included, what measurements were made, and what decisions determined which observations you got to see. If you lose that history, you can produce a very precise answer to the wrong question.

Suppose you have medical data from one hospital and you want to make a decision at another. A confidence interval computed from the first hospital’s data doesn’t, by itself, tell you how well that conclusion transfers. You need to understand the selection process, the measurement process, and what might differ between those settings. Provenance gives you information with which to formulate those questions.

But recording provenance isn’t sufficient either. You have to connect it to assumptions and then ask how sensitive your conclusions are to those assumptions. Sometimes the honest conclusion is that the data don’t identify the quantity you care about. That’s useful uncertainty to communicate, even though it doesn’t take the familiar form of an error bar.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty from selection and transfer between settings, but does not state that older source data should increase an estimate’s uncertainty.

r002.rationale: It says provenance should preserve data-collection history, but does not propose carrying age metadata as data moves through a larger system.
